newsitem.title: THAILAND: Demand for Bangkok office space up mildly - report.
newsitem.headline: Demand for Bangkok office space up mildly - report.

text.p: Demand for office space in Bangkok's central business district showed a modest increase in spite of a recent downturn in the real estate market, property firm Jones Lang Wootton said on Thursday.
Occupancies and average rents increased marginally in the first quarter of this year, it added in a report.

"The improvement seen in the Bangkok CBD (central business district) office market during the first quarter shows that the market fundamentals, though weakening, have not collapsed as many have anticipated and there remains continued occupier demand," it said.
The property sector in Thailand has been depressed because of overbuilding and a liquidity crunch among developers and property firms brought on by high interest rates, analysts said.

The problems in the sector forced the government last month to launch a billion-baht zero coupon bond auction to raise funds to assist cash-strapped property firms and financial institutions with loans to the sector.
Jones Lang Wootton said a total of 53,000 square metres had been occupied over the first quarter. This compared with a similar level achieved over six months in 1996.
"This level of absorption would be considered very healthy in most markets in the region," it said.

There were three projects being completed in the CBD area during the first quarter, which brought the total supply of office space in the area to around 1.53 million square metres, Jones Lang Wootton said.
It expected more than 340,000 square metres of new office space would be completed and enter the market by the end of this year.

"The limited amount of new supply and the high absorption during the first quarter of 1997 resulted in a decline in the average vacancy rate from 14.4 percent as at the end of 1996 to 13.9 percent by April 1," it said.
Average gross rentals have also increased marginally over the quarter to 506 baht ($19.5) per square metre per month, it said.
